items.title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts.

items.title: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. items.title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters.

items.title: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integration. Aggregate population statistics can provide a more task aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient level nearest neighbors f

items.title: Clover 2: dense 27.8B base + 7 LoRA experts routed per token, not a static merge, weights public
items.excerpt: Disclosure: I’m with the team that built this. Wanted to share something a little different from the usual finetune drop. Clover 2 keeps a base model and 7 trained LoRA adapters (roleplay, general assistant, security, math, long-document, efficiency, knowledge) separate at inference time. A trained router picks the right expert(s) per token live, with a null slot that falls back to plain base when nothing specialized applies. So it’s not a merged blend, the model actually makes a decision at every token. Real benchmark gains over the untouched base: meaningful jumps on GSM8K/MATH-500/GSM-Hard, a solid bump on LongBench-v2, and a measurable drop in generic AI-writing tics on creative writing specifically. Everything’s public: base model, all 7 adapters in standard PEFT format, the trained router, and the vLLM plugin to run it with the real per-token behavior: https://huggingface.co/kitaniai/clover-2 Heads up if you’re planning to self-host: no GGUF yet, the hybrid attention architecture’s llama.cpp support is still bleeding-edge. vLLM is the supported path right now. If anyone wants to try it, it's free for the next week at https://kitani.ai/ , with no card required. W

items.title: maxwell-model/Maxwell-V1-Flash · Hugging Face
items.excerpt: Model Introduction Maxwell-V1.0-Flash is a next-generation, high-performance Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model developed by the Maxwell Team, with 35B total parameters and 3B active parameters per token (both excluding embeddings) and support for context lengths up to 256K tokens. It is designed for strong reasoning, agentic, and long-context capabilities at a practical inference cost. Key Features Maxwell Block Sparse Attention (MBSA). Each KV group keeps fixed coverage of 8 prefix and 8 local 128-token blocks and adds up to 16 remote blocks chosen by a learned indexer, bounding main attention at 4,096 tokens per KV group while the full-history KV cache stays available. The MBSA kernel is 6.7x faster than dense GQA at 256K. Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections. Multiple residual streams with learned, input-dependent aggregation and constrained mixing, widening information flow without extra attention or feed-forward evaluations. Fine-Grained Mixture of Experts.
